extra.message: PUT /:id/visibility (updateReviewVisibility) decides whether the caller may hide/unhide ANY review purely from the client-supplied `sharingMode` body field ('vendor_storefront' or 'marketplace_staff') instead of checking the authenticated user's actual role or vendor ownership of the review. Any authenticated buyer can send `{ sharingMode: 'marketplace_staff', hidden: true }` for an arbitrary review id and it will be honored, since only `authenticate` (not `authorize`, and no vendor/staff ownership check) guards this route.

applyMerchandisingFeedPatch (PUT /:id/merchandising-sync) parses an arbitrary JSON object from the `patch` query parameter and applies it directly to the Prisma update via `Object.assign({}, feedPatch)` with no field allowlist. A vendor_manager who owns the product can set ANY column — e.g. `price`, `status` (bypassing admin moderation to force-publish), or `vendorId` (transferring the product to a different vendor). The equivalent admin-only endpoint in routes/admin.ts (applyCatalogFeedPatch) correctly restricts this to a fixed MERCHANDISING_PATCH_FIELDS allowlist; this vendor-facing copy does not.

cwe: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: convertProductExportFormat (POST /:id/export/convert) builds a shell command string by directly interpolating the attacker-controlled `reportType` request body field — `catalog-tools convert --from ${sourcePath} --to ${outputPath} --format ${reportType}` — and executes it with `exec()`, which runs through a shell. Unlike the analogous vendors.ts `convertPayoutStatementFormat` (which validates reportType against a fixed allowlist and uses `spawn(..., { shell:false })` with array args), this handler performs no validation on `reportType`, allowing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or backticks) to be injected and executed on the server.

renderVendorLogoAsset (GET /:id/branding/logo, unauthenticated/public route) builds the file path with `path.join(ASSET_DIR, vendor.logoUrl)` and reads it with `fs.readFileSync` without verifying the resolved path stays inside ASSET_DIR. `vendor.logoUrl` is a vendor-controlled field settable via PUT /vendors/:id (`body('logoUrl').optional().trim()`, no path/URL validation). A vendor can set logoUrl to `../../../../etc/passwd` (or any path) and any unauthenticated visitor can then read arbitrary files off the server's filesystem via this public endpoint. The very next handler, renderVendorBannerAsset, demonstrates the correct fix by checking `requestedPath.startsWith(ASSET_DIR + path.sep)` before reading — that check is missing here.

cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

extra.message: writePayoutLedgerSnapshot (GET /:id/payouts/ledger) takes the `period` query parameter unsanitized and uses it to build the output filename: `path.join(LEDGER_DIR, \`${vendor.id}-${period}.csv\`)`, then calls `fs.writeFileSync`. A caller (any owning vendor_manager or admin) can pass e.g. `period=../../../../tmp/evil` to write attacker-controlled CSV content to an arbitrary path outside LEDGER_DIR. The comparable admin.ts `archiveVendorStatement` handler correctly sanitizes its equivalent label with `path.basename(requestedLabel)` — that protection is absent here.

extra.message: importVendorCatalogAsset builds the destination filename with `${vendor.storeSlug}-catalog.${fileExtension || 'bin'}` where `fileExtension` comes straight from the request body with no validation, then writes it via `path.join(PUBLIC_ASSET_DIR, fileName)` and `fs.writeFileSync`. Supplying `fileExtension: '../../../../var/www/html/shell.php'` (or similar) escapes PUBLIC_ASSET_DIR and writes the fetched remote content to an arbitrary path, which combined with the SSRF below can plant attacker-controlled content anywhere on disk the process can write.

cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

extra.message: importVendorCatalogAsset performs `fetch(assetUrl)` where `assetUrl` is taken directly from the request body with no allowlist, scheme restriction, or private-IP/metadata-endpoint filtering. An admin-triggered request lets an attacker who controls the assetUrl value (e.g. via a compromised/malicious vendor onboarding submission workflow) make the server issue requests to internal-only services or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254) and have the response contents written to disk and returned indirectly.

importVendorComplianceDocument performs `fetch(documentUrl)` where `documentUrl` is taken directly from the request body with no allowlist or private-network filtering (only the resulting Content-Length and a MIME allowlist are checked after the fact). This allows the server to be used as a proxy to reach internal-only network services or cloud metadata endpoints.

draftDisputeResolutionSuggestion embeds the buyer-controlled `dispute.description` (free text supplied when the dispute was created, fully attacker-controlled) directly into an LLM prompt asking it to end its answer with 'RESOLUTION: REFUND' or 'RESOLUTION: DENY'. The handler then regex-matches the model's raw output for `/RESOLUTION:\s*REFUND/i` and, if found, automatically marks the dispute resolved and refunds the order in a transaction — bypassing all of the checks the legitimate PUT /:id/resolve endpoint performs (status validation, staff-only authorization re-check at action time, and buyer/vendor notification). A buyer can craft the dispute description to manipulate the LLM into emitting the trigger string (classic prompt injection via untrusted content embedded in a prompt whose output directly drives a privileged financial action), forcing an unauthorized refund.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

extra.message: acceptDisputeResolutionOffer decrypts the caller-supplied `offerToken` using AES-256-CBC with no integrity/authentication tag, then distinguishes decryption failures by message content: a 'bad decrypt'/padding-related error returns 'Offer token padding is invalid' while any other failure returns a different generic message. Returning a distinguishable response for padding-validity failures versus other failures is the classic precondition for a padding oracle attack, letting an attacker iteratively decrypt or forge ciphertext without knowing RESOLUTION_OFFER_KEY. Contrast with the adjacent confirmOrderDelivery handler in orders.ts, which uses authenticated AES-256-GCM and explicitly collapses every decryption failure mode into one identical response so nothing leaks.

cwe: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

extra.message: recalculateOrderTotals returns the full internal error message, stack trace, and echoed query string to the client whenever the request includes `?context=diagnostic`, with no additional authorization beyond the normal order-access check. Any buyer, vendor, or admin with access to a given order can trigger an internal error path (e.g. via a malformed request) and append this flag to obtain a raw stack trace, exposing internal file paths and implementation details.

cwe: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

extra.message: onboardSupportDeskAccount hashes the new staff member's temporary credential with `bcrypt.hash(tempCredential, strength || 4)` where `strength` is taken directly from the request body as a number with no bounds validation. A caller can pass an arbitrarily low cost factor (e.g. `strength: 1`), producing a weakly-hashed credential that is far cheaper to brute-force than the marketplace's standard work factor of 12 used everywhere else (e.g. onboardVendorTeamMember in vendors.ts hardcodes 12).

cwe: CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

extra.message: verifyPayoutDestination logs the entire request body via `console.warn('Payout destination verification failed', req.body)` when the banking partner rejects the submission. Since this endpoint's body carries the vendor's payout/banking destination details, this writes sensitive financial account information to application logs in plaintext.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

extra.message: previewOrderAutoReplyMessage compiles a vendor-supplied string directly with `Handlebars.compile(messageTemplate)` and renders it. Compiling arbitrary caller-controlled templates with a full-featured template engine is inherently risky (server-side template injection surface, potential for prototype-pollution-style helper abuse depending on runtime environment/version) — the safe pattern used elsewhere in this codebase (see notifications.ts DIGEST_GREETING_TEMPLATE) is to compile a fixed, developer-authored template string and only interpolate data into it, never compile caller-supplied template source.

extra.message: The API-key authentication branch looks up `prisma.apiKey.findFirst({ where: { keyHash: token, ... } })`, comparing the raw, caller-supplied token directly against the `keyHash` column. If this column is meant to store a hash of the actual secret (as its name implies), no hashing of the incoming token is ever performed before the comparison, meaning `keyHash` must actually contain the plaintext key for any match to succeed — i.e. API keys are effectively stored and compared in plaintext rather than hashed.
